newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Violence erupts after protest against Euro-drive.
newsitem.headline: Violence erupts after protest against Euro-drive.

text.p: Protesters and police clashed on Saturday as violence erupted at the end of a street march against hardship wrought by Europe's quest for monetary union.
Witnesses said up to 150 demonstrators went on the rampage, smashing windows, overturning a patrol car and pelting riot police with stones in Amsterdam's city centre.
They said some demonstrators tried unsuccessfully to storm the heavily-guarded Dutch Central Bank, which is hosting a summit of European Union leaders on Monday and Tuesday.
Earlier, between 35,000 and 50,000 people from across Europe turned Amsterdam into a sea of red and black, marching to protest against the drive toward European economic integration.
During the 45 minutes of violence, fireworks were set off, bystanders were attacked and police made a handful of arrests.
"They're smashing the windows of the ABN AMRO bank. Police and marchers are scuffling. A couple of people have been arrested. There are also ambulances on the scene," a Reuters photographer said.
Police played down the extent of the trouble, saying only that one man was arrested after the skirmishes and that the situation had quickly returned to normal.
"There are no big problems," spokesman Klaas Wilting said, adding that 500-600 police had been on hand to control the crowd, which he estimated at 50,000.

Organisers of the European Marches Against Unemployment, Poverty and Social Exclusion said about 35,000 people jammed the central Dam square before walking through the streets to send a message to European leaders due here on Sunday evening.
"All the summit is going to talk about is money," said Lot van Baaren, one of the Dutch organisers.
"These people are here because they want a social Europe...one that puts people back on the agenda."
Austerity measures imposed in many states to try to qualify for the European single currency have seen the bloc's jobless rate rising and stoked popular resentment against the Union.

Among banners at the march proclaiming "No to the bosses of Europe, No to slave labour" and "Amsterdam - listen to the voice of the people," were hundreds of others bearing the simple legend "No to the euro" in all the bloc's languages.
"We're heading for a big catastrophe and our leaders just don't seem to understand," said French marcher Michel Bouchon. "For us, Europe must be social or we don't want to have Europe."

The new Socialist government in France has been pushing for an initiative to promote economic growth and jobs to be included in a new EU treaty due to be signed at the Amsterdam summit, as a counterweight to a pact on limiting budget deficits.
Countries such as France and Germany have been struggling to restrict their deficits to the level laid down in the Maastricht Treaty, pressurising public spending.

"From Maastricht on, we have been promised that Europe will mean more prosperity for the average person, but that is not true," said Anja Deschoemacker from Belgium. "All it has meant is more profits for all the big companies."
"Why should we welcome a new treaty when the governments already use Maastricht as an excuse to avoid spending any money on their people."
Many demonstators said Europe was failing to address other pressing social issues, with large groups protesting the bloc's immigration and environmental policies.
"At the moment, I guess I think Europe is a bad thing overall," said Julia Schindler from Germany. "But particularly because of the lack of attention for the environment.
Security was tight along the route of the march through central Amsterdam, with white-helmeted riot police stationed on the canals leading off the main streets.
